name: Vitamin B12 / anemia correction

card.summary: Treating B12 deficiency or anemia is standard medicine; any appearance gain (paleness, dark circles) applies only where deficiency is the cause.
card.note: Supplementation benefits are established for deficiency; evidence for appearance benefits in people without it is not documented in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause anemia, pale skin, hair color changes, mouth problems and neurological symptoms, and is treated with oral or injected B12. Looksmaxxing discussion links correcting anemia to fixing pallor and under-eye circles.

References note that iron and B12 deficiency are believed to contribute to dark circles by making skin paler so vessels show through. That applies to people who are deficient; supplementing without a deficiency has not been shown in these sources to change appearance.
quick.mechanism: B12 is needed for DNA synthesis in blood-cell formation; deficiency produces large, poorly functioning red cells (megaloblastic anemia). Correcting the deficiency restores red-cell production.
quick.risks: Folic acid can mask B12-deficiency anemia while nerve damage progresses, and some neurological damage can be permanent if untreated. Diagnosis and treatment route (oral versus injection) are medical decisions; severe cases usually start with injections.

lead: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a recognised medical condition caused most often by impaired absorption (for example pernicious anemia, gastric surgery, some medications), by inadequate intake in vegans, or by increased need. It produces megaloblastic anemia, and symptoms can include pale skin, hair color changes, mouth ulcers, fatigue and neurological problems [1].

Reference material on dark circles states that iron and B12 deficiency are believed to contribute, as pallor can make underlying veins more visible [2]. In appearance communities this is the basis for correcting anemia as a route to a healthier look.
Treatment of deficiency is well established, and lifelong B12 is usually recommended if no reversible cause is found [1].

paras: Pernicious anemia, an autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor, is the leading cause in developed countries and affects about 2 to 3 percent of people over 65 [1]. Other contributors include gastrectomy, gastric bypass, Crohn's and coeliac disease, long-term use of proton pump inhibitors or metformin, and nitrous oxide exposure [1].
Blood findings include macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Folic acid can mask the anemia while neurological damage continues [1].

Listed deficiency signs include pale skin, premature greying and color changes in skin including dark circles under the eyes [1]. Dark circles have many other causes, including pigmentation, allergy, thin skin and fatigue [2].

Treatment uses oral or injected B12, with severe cases usually starting with injections. A 2019 study cited by Wikipedia suggested oral B12 is inferior in severe cases, and a 2018 Cochrane review compared routes [1].

Thomas Addison described pernicious anemia in the nineteenth century. In the 1920s George Whipple found liver cured blood-loss anemia in dogs, and in 1934 Whipple, William Murphy and George Minot shared the Nobel Prize for liver-based treatment, later found to contain large amounts of B12 [1].

No studies found on B12 or anemia correction for cosmetic outcomes. Registered trials of iron and anemia management exist in other settings, such as daily oral iron for iron deficiency (NCT05185024), but they do not address appearance [3].

timeline.event: Thomas Addison begins describing pernicious anemia. [1]
Whipple, Murphy and Minot receive the Nobel Prize for liver therapy, later linked to B12. [1]
